content.name: p
children: An auditor asks a harder question than “what grants are in our YAML?”:

children.name: strong
children: can this role actually perform the operation?
Acme’s role graph is tidy, but PostgreSQL has access paths outside ordinary named ACLs.

content.name: p
children: Before changing anything, use the lab to identify the unexpected path, name the role or object that makes it possible, repair that path, and repeat the affected login's query as a negative test.

content.name: p
children: on new functions by default. State both desired absences so existing and future functions converge:

content.name: Fence
children:
grants:
  - role: PUBLIC
    ensure: absent
    privileges: [EXECUTE]
    object: { type: function, schema: billing_api, name: "*" }

default_privileges:
  - owner: app_owner
    scope: { type: global }
    grant:
      - role: PUBLIC
        ensure: absent
        privileges: [EXECUTE]
        on_type: function

content.name: p
children: The global default matters because PostgreSQL’s built-in function default is global. A schema-scoped revoke cannot subtract a global grant.

content.name: p

content.name: p
children: One more finding costs nothing to write down: Acme’s application still connects with the founder-era admin credentials, and a superuser bypasses every check in this chapter. No grant, policy, or RLS rule constrains that connection—pgroles cannot manage it away. Moving the application onto a scoped login, the way
was built in chapter 2, is the remediation an auditor will ask for first.
